asDecan.p: Leo gets cut into three slices of ten degrees, and your Sun is in the last one, somewhere from 20 to 29 degrees. The Golden Dawn gave that slice to Mars. Mars has no particular standing in Leo. It isn't at home there and it isn't weakened either, so it behaves like a guest in the Sun's house and picks up some of the Sun's manners. Leo is fixed fire, and fixed signs are the ones that stay put, so Mars arriving late in the sign makes a fighter whose instinct is to hold ground once it has some. The slices before it fill in the rest. The Five of Wands is Saturn and a lot of scrappy effort. The Six is Jupiter and the victory parade. By the Seven the parade's over and somebody wants your spot. You're also at the very end of the sign, with Virgo next, and late Leos usually have some of Virgo's carefulness in them. Strength is Leo's Major, so that card's yours as well, and the Seven is the narrower reading of it for these ten degrees.

You notice very quickly when someone's edging onto your ground. A new hire starts copying your manager into emails about a project you set up, and by lunchtime you've drafted the reply in your head. At a family dinner your uncle has a go at your job, or your haircut, or the fact you still rent, and you don't let it slide the way the rest of the table does. You answer him, politely, with facts. In a group chat where everyone's piling onto one friend, you're usually the one who types 'hang on, that's a bit unfair' and then watches the dots appear. None of this feels like aggression from the inside. It feels like basic housekeeping. Mars in the Sun's sign fights out in the open, so people always know where you stand, and to be honest you'd find it hard to hide even if you tried.

You don't need a crowd behind you, and that's rarer than it sounds. Plenty of people will stand up for something once the room has turned their way. You'll do it at five to one, in a body corporate meeting where everyone wants the cheaper quote and you're the only person who read the engineer's report. Have a look at the man on the card. He's outnumbered, his shoes don't even match, and he's still up there. Once you've said the unpopular thing, someone quieter usually pipes up with 'actually, I agree', and they'd never have gone first. You give other people the nerve without meaning to. You're also right a fair bit of the time. That's the Virgo end of Leo showing, and it means you've usually checked the figures before you open your mouth.

You can get so used to being challenged that peace makes you twitchy. A few months with nothing to push against, a job where everyone agrees with you, a relationship that's simply going well, and you'll find something anyway. The neighbour's new fence starts to look like a statement. The small points are the other trouble. You'll give way on the big things if someone properly shows you you're wrong, but the tiny ones, who said they'd book the restaurant, whether the film started at seven or half past, you defend like a border. Apologies tend to come out sideways, as a cup of tea left on someone's desk or the dishes done without being asked, and the person who was waiting for the actual words doesn't always get them.

A loss, an unfair review, a friend who takes the other side, and the first thing you do is fight. You ring HR the same afternoon, you write the long email, you tell your partner exactly what you should have said in the meeting and then tell them again in the car. There's a lot of heat in that first day and some of it is useful. A week later it usually hasn't gone anywhere. It's moved into your shoulders and your sleep, and you're still arguing with people who've mostly moved on. The ones closest to you get tired of hearing about it, and a few start to feel that disagreeing with you on anything is risky. What helps is physical first. Mars needs somewhere to go, so a hard run or a long swim will do more for you than another conversation. After that, ask someone you trust whether this one is still worth holding.

You can be territorial about your place in someone's life. The ex who still texts on their birthday, the best friend who's known them since primary school, the colleague they mention a bit too often, and you notice every time one of them seems to rank above you. You won't always say so. It comes out as a sharp question about Saturday's plans. You also need some resistance. A partner who agrees with everything will bore you inside a couple of months, though you'd never admit it, and Mars with nothing to push against goes looking in the wrong places, the tone of a text, the way they said goodnight. You do best with someone who'll argue with you over dinner and have forgotten it by dessert. If you're with a gentle person, tell them it's fine to disagree with you, and don't sulk when they do.

You work best when there's something specific to hold. A brand you built, a budget line, a client you brought in, a standard nobody else will keep. Give you that and you'll defend it through three restructures. Jobs that suit this slice of Leo often have some advocacy in them, the lawyer, the union delegate, the editor who won't let marketing rewrite the headline, the head chef who sends a plate back. It goes wrong in the job with no clear ground, all consensus and shared ownership and workshops, where you end up defending things that were never yours to begin with. Keep an eye on the moment a colleague's suggestion lands as an attack on your work. Usually it isn't one. When it genuinely is, put your case in writing, calmly, with the numbers attached, and send it to the person who can actually decide.

At twenty this decan fights almost everything. The lecturer who marked you down, the flatmate who used your milk, the manager who didn't listen in your first week. A lot of it is fair, and some of it is just Mars in a young body with nowhere to put it. By the mid-thirties most people with a late Leo Sun have lost a couple of fights that mattered and won a couple that didn't, and that's usually what teaches the sorting. You get choosier. You still stand up, just less often, and people take it more seriously when you do. The fifties often bring a funny shift. Having stood on your own so many times, you become the person others ring when they're outnumbered, and a lot of your fighting gets done on someone else's behalf. I've seen this decan make very good mentors, especially for people starting out in a field that isn't kind to newcomers.

Before you answer a challenge, a snippy email, a comment at dinner, a rival's pitch, give it a score out of ten for how much it actually matters to you. Write the number on a sticky note if it's a message, or just say it in your head. Anything under six gets a short, friendly reply or none at all. Six and above, you fight properly, but you sleep on it first and answer in the morning. Keep a tally for a month and count how many sixes there really were.
